summary: Addresses the key management side of the TCP MD5 Signature Option, used mostly by BGP. Its security depends heavily on the quality of the keys used to compute the signature, so the document discusses the requirements for that keying material. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A TCP MD5 signature is only useful if its secret key is difficult to guess and does not reach too many people. RFC 3562 recommends key sizes, replacement intervals and safer handling practices.

questions: how long should a tcp md5 key be
how often should bgp md5 keys change
what is tcp md5 signature option
subtitle: Key length, lifetime and sharing advice for the TCP MD5 Signature Option.

tldr.problem: The TCP MD5 Signature Option's security depends heavily on its secret key, and attackers may try to guess that key.
tldr.mechanism: The memo estimates key-guessing capability and recommends long random keys, limited sharing between peerings, and regular key changes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3562 provides key-management guidance for the option in RFC 2385. It is Informational and does not define a new protocol.

today: RFC 3562 is an Informational memo published in July 2003. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Key Management Matters
sections.content:
The TCP MD5 Signature Option, defined in RFC 2385 and used predominantly by BGP, relies on keying material to calculate its signature. The memo considers key guessing the main threat for the option and recommends keys between 12 and 24 bytes, limited to a single BGP peering arrangement, and changed at least every 90 days.

The recommendations use SHOULD language. They are guidance about keys used by the existing option, not a new TCP mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The option's protection depends on the secret used to calculate its signature. The memo recommends long keys, limited sharing and regular replacement.

sections.title: Estimating Key-Guessing Speed
sections.content:
The memo estimates how quickly an attacker might test candidate keys. It starts from an earlier MD5 software measurement and projects a higher rate for the period around 2002. It also considers attacks spread across many computers and specialized hardware.

For the analysis, the attacker is assumed to target short packets. The memo estimates that a distributed attack could perform between 1.0e11 and 1.0e13 MD5 operations per second, while noting that these values depend on its assumptions.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo estimates key strength by considering how many guesses an attacker might make. Its estimates include multiple computers and specialized hardware, not just one machine.

sections.title: Entropy, Length and Key Lifetime
sections.content:
Assuming a 90-day replacement interval and a software attack rate of 1.0e13 MD5 operations per second, the memo estimates a minimum of about 68 bits of key entropy. It rounds this up to at least 80 bits, or 10 bytes. Under its hardware-attack assumptions, it rounds the recommended minimum length to 12 bytes.

Human-language keys provide less entropy per character than random keys. The memo recommends generating a high-quality random key of 96 bits or more and choosing the largest practical key length below 25 bytes, while using at least 12 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Random keys are harder to guess than keys made from ordinary words. The memo recommends at least 12 bytes and favors random keys with 96 bits or more of entropy.

sections.title: Implementation and Key Handling
sections.content:
Some implementations limit keys to short ASCII strings. The memo warns that word-like keys may have very little entropy and can be vulnerable to dictionary attacks. Implementations SHOULD allow direct binary keys, SHOULD NOT impose unnecessary length limits, and SHOULD allow keys of at least 16 bytes.

Anyone holding a shared key can forge packets that appear to come from another holder. The memo therefore recommends limiting a key to two parties. When keys are transported electronically, secure handling MUST be used; it recommends protocols such as S/MIME, TLS or SSH where appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: Short word-based keys are easier to guess, and everyone who holds a key can forge packets for the others. Support long binary keys and share each key with as few parties as practical.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
The memo addresses security requirements for keying material used with RFC 2385. It says that the document creates no new security exposures.

RFC 3562 is an Informational memo that provides operational guidance; it does not define a protocol or guarantee that a key is safe when it is weak or widely shared.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo gives security guidance for keys used with the TCP MD5 Signature Option. It does not add a new protocol or remove the risks of weak or exposed keys.
